title: The 'three columns': Jansenists accept a sense of the third condemned proposition, yet require freedom from necessity
source_text: XXXVI. In illo vero scripto quod vocant trium columnarum, ubi distinguunt varios sensus quinque famosarum propositionum, quas damnarunt Pontifices Romani Innocentius X. & Alexander VII. tertiae propositioni hunc sensum tanquam bonum & sibi probatum tribuunt. Ad merendum & demerendum, in statu naturae lapsae, non requiritur in homine libertas a necessitate infallibilitatis, sed sufficit Libertas a coactione cum judicio rationis, si consideretur praecise essentia libertatis & meriti, quanquam ex ratione status semper reperiatur indifferentia potentiae, qua voluntas, etiam sub gratia proxime necessaria & ex se efficaci potest non velle, non tamen ut unquam simul cum eadem gratia non velit. Ubi agnoscunt semper in statu naturae lapsae, Libertati adjunctam esse voluntatis indifferentiam. Et propterea in articulis illis Convenarum Episcopo oblatis, non verentur dicere, Quod ad merendum & demerendum in statu naturae lapsae non sufficit Libertas a coactione; sed requiritur libertas a necessitate. Quamvis enim, inquiunt, gratia per se efficax infallibiliter & insuperabiliter voluntatem ad agendum determinet, atque ita nunquam voluntas illi actu dissentiat; non tamen inducit necessitatem, quia non tollit dissentiendi potestatem.
pass_a_gloss: But in that writing which they call of the three columns, where they distinguish the various senses of the five famous propositions which the Roman Pontiffs Innocent X. and Alexander VII. condemned, to the third proposition they attribute this sense as good and approved by them. For meriting and demeriting, in the state of fallen nature, there is not required in man liberty from the necessity of infallibility, but Liberty from compulsion with the judgment of reason suffices, if the essence of liberty and merit be considered precisely, although by reason of the state there is always found an indifference of power, by which the will, even under grace proximately necessary and of itself efficacious, can not will, yet not so that it ever at the same time with the same grace does not will. Where they acknowledge that always in the state of fallen nature, indifference of the will is joined to Liberty. And therefore in those articles offered to the Bishop of Comminges, they do not fear to say, That for meriting and demeriting in the state of fallen nature Liberty from compulsion does not suffice; but liberty from necessity is required. For although, they say, grace efficacious of itself infallibly and insuperably determines the will to act, and so the will never in act dissents from it; yet it does not induce necessity, because it does not take away the power of dissenting.
pass_b_english: In the paper they call 'of the three columns', where they separate the different senses of the five well-known propositions condemned by the popes Innocent X and Alexander VII, they assign to the third proposition the following sense as sound and accepted by them.

'To merit and demerit in the state of fallen nature, man does not need freedom from the necessity of infallibility. Freedom from compulsion together with the judgment of reason is enough, if one considers strictly the essence of freedom and of merit. Yet given the condition of that state, there is always an indifference of power by which the will, even under grace that is proximately necessary and efficacious of itself, is able not to will, though never so as not to will while under that same grace.'
Here they grant that in the state of fallen nature indifference of the will always goes with freedom.

That is why, in the articles presented to the bishop of Comminges, they do not hesitate to say: 'To merit and demerit in the state of fallen nature, freedom from compulsion is not enough; freedom from necessity is required. For although grace efficacious of itself determines the will to act infallibly and irresistibly, so that the will never actually dissents from it, it does not bring in necessity, since it does not remove the power of dissenting.'
